node.label: Constance Backhouse
node.date_label: Petticoats and Prejudice (1991) · Colour-Coded (1999) · Carnal Crimes (2008)
node.description: In Colour-Coded (1999), Constance Backhouse argued that Canadian law created and maintained racial hierarchy, challenging the national mythology that Canada was largely free of racism. In Petticoats and Prejudice (1991), she used individual women’s encounters with courts, family law and employment law to show how legal institutions organized gender inequality. Her case histories connect legal rules to the people who administered, contested and endured them; Colour-Coded also acknowledges that her earlier work had not adequately examined race alongside gender. Petticoats won the Law and Society Association’s J. Willard Hurst Prize in 1992. Greg Marquis’s 1992 review called it “groundbreaking” and said it “opens a number of doors,” while noting that “some may quibble with the representativeness” of its cases, that class “takes a back seat to gender,” and that the Maritimes receive about eight per cent of the study. Carnal Crimes (2008) later extended her case-study approach to sexual assault law in twentieth-century Canada.
node.representative_figures_and_works: Petticoats and Prejudice: Women and Law in Nineteenth-Century Canada (1991; second edition 2015); Challenging Times: The Women’s Movement in Canada and the United States (1992), coedited with David H. node.scope_note: Colour-Coded read selectively: acknowledgments, introduction, selected printed notes, opening of chapter 2 and first two conclusion pages; extended acknowledgments note 2 read by OCR. Petticoats and Prejudice read through Marquis’s review and publisher materials; the book itself unread. Carnal Crimes front matter and author description only. Srigley’s review supplies a mediated Sangster attribution; Sangster’s book unread. Other selected books identified from author and institutional bibliographies, not read in full.

proposed_edges.relationship: In Colour-Coded (1999), Backhouse uses Higginbotham’s “African-American Women’s History and the Metalanguage of Race” (1992) to reject accounts that assume dominant and subordinated groups understood racial hierarchy alike.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Introduction p. 11 (PDF p. 26), first two paragraphs, and printed note 13, p. 285 (PDF p. 300). Backhouse invokes Higginbotham on how racial meanings were “internalized”, in her argument that subordinate communities resisted claims of inferiority. Higginbotham’s original article was not independently read here; the edge records Backhouse’s own explicit use.

proposed_edges.relationship: Petticoats and Prejudice (1991) made individual women’s encounters with marriage, fertility, family, work and criminal law a history of how Canadian law organized gender inequality, as Greg Marquis’s 1992 review explains.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Marquis, p. 171 (PDF p. 10), the paragraph devoted to Petticoats calls its conclusion “patriarchal” and discusses both legal incapacity and the case method. Read the review and Osgoode’s contents/description, not the book. This is an attributed contribution to Canadian women’s history, not a claim that Backhouse founded the field.

proposed_edges.relationship: Colour-Coded (1999) argues that Canadian legislators and courts created and maintained racial hierarchy, making law an active agent in the history of racism rather than a neutral background.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Introduction pp. 13–17, especially p. 15 (PDF p. 30), describes law as a “systemic instrument” of oppression and specifies racial classification, immigration and segregation. These pages were directly read in the author-posted original text; the whole book was not read. Contribution concerns the field’s legal construction of race strand, not immigration alone.

proposed_edges.relationship: Petticoats and Prejudice (1991) examines the legal regulation of marriage, courtship, sexual violence, fertility and prostitution, including labour laws that controlled working women’s sexuality, as Marquis’s 1992 review describes.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Marquis, p. 171 (PDF p. 10), paragraph on Petticoats, characterizes protective labour law as “controlling the sexuality” of working-class women. Osgoode contents corroborate the selected domains. The book is unread; this scoped field contribution does not identify Backhouse with Corrigan’s or Valverde’s theoretical framework.
proposed_edges.map_label: Legal regulation of sexuality and family

proposed_edges.relationship: In Carnal Crimes (2008), Backhouse says her book builds on earlier Canadian research on sexual assault, crediting Dubinsky’s Improper Advances (1993) with supporting a feminist analysis of the power dynamics of sexual violence and with showing that women were not silent victims but active in negotiating their own sexual encounters.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read the Introduction of Carnal Crimes: Sexual Assault Law in Canada, 1900–1975 (Irwin Law for the Osgoode Society, 2008; © 2008), pp. 3–14, in the author-deposited PDF of the paperback printing on the author’s own website. On p. 12 (PDF p. 24), in the paragraph beginning “This book builds upon the path-breaking research of other Canadian historians who have explored sexual assault”, the body text states: “Karen Dubinsky’s study of sexual crime in northern and rural Ontario supported a feminist analysis of the power dynamics of sexual violence, and it emphasized that women were not silent victims, but active in negotiating their own sexual encounters.” Note 28 (p. 302, PDF p. 314) identifies the work as Improper Advances: Rape and Heterosexual Conflict in Ontario, 1880–1929 (Chicago, 1993). The paragraph then says “This study expands upon the work of these earlier researchers with a specifically legal focus”. The same paragraph names other historians (Chapman, Erickson, Chunn, Phillips, Cliche, Olsen, Connor, Strange, Sangster, Ross, Adams, Chenier), but Dubinsky is the only one whose argument, rather than subject, is characterised. This body-text statement of debt and argument is not an acknowledgment list or a collective “see” note. Chapter 4 also quotes Dubinsky (p. 97, n. 51, Improper Advances pp. 132–33) on contemporary views of male sexuality, without naming her in the body; that is not relied on. Dubinsky’s book was not read.

proposed_edges.relationship: In Carnal Crimes (2008), Backhouse frames her nine twentieth-century Canadian sexual-assault cases as “a multi-dimensional examination of the forces of intersectionality” and argues that they bear out the premise that intersectional factors played a definitive role in women’s historical experiences of sexual assault.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Carnal Crimes, Introduction, pp. 11–12 (PDF pp. 23–24). On p. 11 Backhouse summarises the critique by critical race scholars of the universality of “gender”: “not all women experienced sexual assault the same way” (n. 23 lists the scholars). On p. 12, in the paragraph beginning “The cases profiled here provide strong support”, she writes that “the cases in this study also amply bear out the premise that intersectional factors played a definitive role in women’s historical experiences of sexual assault”. In the next paragraph she says the book “contains a multi-dimensional examination of the forces of intersectionality”, which distinguishes it from earlier regional studies. This is the author’s own statement of her method and finding in her own book. The case chapters were not reread for this edge, and no claim is made about how the intersectional analysis works in each chapter. Some chapters concern cases with Indigenous complainants or accused; this edge relies only on the introduction, and nothing is said about those cases (OCAP care).
proposed_edges.map_label: Intersectional legal history of sexual assault

proposed_edges.relationship: Constance Backhouse and Adele Perry were two of the four co-editors, with Cynthia E. Milton and Margaret Kovach, of Royally Wronged: The Royal Society of Canada and Indigenous Peoples (2021), a twelve-essay scholarly collection examining the Royal Society of Canada's complicity in colonialism.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read Andrew Nurse’s review on the BC Studies journal website, especially the editorial attribution immediately below the title, the paragraph beginning “The result is a collection of twelve essays”, and Publication Information. The attribution explicitly identifies Backhouse and Perry as editors of the same book; Publication Information supplies the 2021 original publication year. The review describes a substantive scholarly essay collection, including an editorial introduction and afterword. Backhouse’s own Books page independently confirms the co-editorship in the Royally Wronged section. This edge asserts collaboration as co-editors, without assigning shared authorship of individual chapters or inferring intellectual influence. The underlying book is unread. OCAP scope: published editorial collaboration and scholarship only; no community knowledge, oral narratives, narrator quotations, ceremonies, genealogies or identity claims are included.
proposed_edges.map_label: Co-editors (with Milton and Kovach) of Royally Wronged (2021)

proposed_edges.relationship: In Manly Militants, Cohesive Communities, and Defiant Domestics (1995), Franca Iacovetta discusses Petticoats and Prejudice (1991) as an example of sophisticated legal history integrating racial-ethnic differences into gender analysis.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Journal-hosted historiographical essay read at pp. 249–252, with its opening framing at pp. 217–219. The body names Backhouse and explains the book's treatment of differences among women. Recorded as a favorable published appraisal, without inferring a personal intellectual debt.

proposed_edges.relationship: Colour-Coded (1999) contributed to racial-formation history by analyzing racial categories' instability and racialization's continuing effects, as Tracey Lindberg's review (2001) explains.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Review evidence only; pp. 199–200 read. No theoretical-school affiliation inferred.

proposed_edges.relationship: Tracey Lindberg's review (2001) judges that Colour-Coded (1999), by acknowledging First Nations systems of law alongside Canadian law, becomes 'in a sense, an anti-colonial' work, while calling it a largely successful but inconsistent attempt.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Review pp. 197–198 read; Lindberg also qualifies its treatment of governance. Scholarship only.
